newsitem.title: USA: SPECTRUM OF FOREIGN CRUDES HANGING OVER U.S. GULF.
newsitem.headline: SPECTRUM OF FOREIGN CRUDES HANGING OVER U.S. GULF.

text.p: Both sweet and sour foreign crudes hung over the U.S. Gulf Coast on Monday, offering refiners a wide selection to fill their September requirements, traders said.
On the sweet end of the market, Colombian state oil company Ecopetrol sold a pair of Cusiana cargoes last Friday in an increasingly sloppy market.

A cargo loading September 11-15 was sold to a U.S. refiner at around October West Texas Intermediate/Cushing minus $1.05. A separate cargo loading September 29 to October 3 was sold to another U.S. refiner at around November WTI minus $1.02, traders said.

Meanwhile, an equity producer was heard to have swapped its cargo loading September 9-13 for a U.S. refiner's cargo loading September 14-18. The deal allows the equity producer to offer two cargoes loading September 14-18 and 15-19 as possible co-loaders, traders said.
Another U.S. refiner was heard re-offering its Cusiana loading September 3-7, asking parity to October WTI.
So far, six of 15 Cusiana cargoes in the September program have been sold, with two of those currently being re-offered into the market, traders said.
The Cusiana market was pegged at Oct WTI minus $1.05-1.10 a barrel, down sharply from a late August range of Oct WTI minus 55-60 cents.
The plethora of Cusiana crude seems to have helped keep North Sea Brent offers at bay, traders said.
"Brent offers have receded," a Gulf trader said. "Sellers are afraid of bringing a VLCC over and only selling a cargo or two."
The trader assessed the notional level of delivered Brent at WTI minus 30 cents a barrel.

Meanwhile, several West African cargoes slated for late-August arrival have yet to be sold, putting more downward pressure on sweet crude prices in the late-August to early-September timeframe, traders said.
On the sour end of the market, at least two cargoes of Iraqi crude have already been sold into the Gulf Coast, traders said.

A trading house sold Basrah Light to a U.S. refiner for end-September arrival at around November WTI minus $2.00 a barrel. A Kirkuk cargo was also sold at around October WTI minus $1.80, traders said.

Iraqi exports are expected to get underway this week under the U.N. oil-for-food program. Baghdad said on Monday it plans to sell 30 million barrels in the remaining weeks of the first 90-day period of the program, equivalent to some 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd).
Among other sour grades, Ecopetrol on Monday lifted force majeure on exports of Cano Limon crude. Two U.S.-bound cargoes were affected, with eight to 10 delays anticipated.
Elsewhere in Latin America, an Argentine producer was offering 380,000 barrels of Escalante crude loading September 22-23, asking October WTI minus $4.20 a barrel.
